clue.text: Money once put into exercise area

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
put means set, as in set something down

explanation.surface: Somebody tucks coins away in the gym or exercise yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' signals the container. 'Money once' points to a former currency, not cash spent in the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: The peseta was the currency of Spain before the euro replaced it, hence money of a former time.

clue.text: Tire out going up and down

indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads identically from top to bottom and from bottom to top

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Something is worn out from all the climbing up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up and down' says the four-letter word is the same read upwards or downwards in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To poop someone is informal British slang for exhausting them, as in feeling pooped.

clue.text: Silly boy checking Irish guy's pulse

indicators.note: checking is read as holding something in check, keeping it held inside

parts.note: Sean is a typical Irish man's name

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters behave foolishly and get rearranged

explanation.surface: A foolish lad is taking an Irishman's pulse, like a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' is the anagram signal and 'checking' the container signal. 'pulse' looks like a heartbeat being taken, but it means an edible seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes, and the soya bean is one of them.

clue.text: A "GOD" — he'd Tyke folk run round to order!

definitions.text: A "GOD" — he'd Tyke folk run round to order!

indicators.note: putting things to order means arranging them, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
taken as written
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a run
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire grandee orders his local troops to march around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to order' is the anagram signal, with run as R. A Tyke is a Yorkshireman, and A GOD reads as Grand Old Duke, like GOM for Grand Old Man; the nursery-rhyme duke made his men march up and down.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the nursery-rhyme commander, a Yorkshire nobleman ordering his men to march round.

clue.text: Final stage of house extension?

parts.note: a house is a home
an extension is a stretch, a lengthening

explanation.surface: Someone is near the end of building an extension on their house.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a building job nearly done; split the answer into two words for house and extension.
explanation.definitionFit: The last straight before a racecourse finish line, used figuratively for the closing phase of anything.

clue.text: Maybe wearing some larger undies …

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone may be wearing a bigger size of underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs this clue on into 7 down for the story only. 'Maybe' signals an example: 'wearing' as a verbal noun is one instance.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb form ending in -ing used as a noun is this part of speech, and 'wearing' can serve as one.

clue.text: … pretends to have topping bottom amongst bottoms?

indicators.note: amongst says one piece sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: asses is slang for backsides, bottoms

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top, here the first letter

parts.note: a bum is a backside, a bottom

explanation.surface: A cheeky line continuing the underwear story about one bottom on top of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topping' removes the first letter and 'amongst' is the container signal. The ellipsis links this clue to 6 down's underwear story only.
explanation.definitionFit: To assume a manner or air is to put it on falsely, which is to pretend.

clue.text: 60% of dirty nappies almost get thrown in a waste disposal unit

indicators.note: things that get thrown are flung about, so the letters are mixed up
sixty per cent of a five-letter word keeps its first three letters
almost means nearly all, so the final letter is lost

explanation.surface: Soiled nappies are tossed into a household waste unit.
explanation.walkthrough: '60% of' keeps DIR and 'almost' cuts NAPPIES to NAPPIE; 'get thrown' rearranges DIRNAPPIE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe that carries away rainwater or sewage is a unit for getting rid of waste.

Food (or drink) initially making bloke randy or incontinent?

annotationWithheld.why: Food (or drink) initially making bloke randy or incontinent? (8): the parse puts MBRO (initials) inside ASIA, with 'incontinent' read as 'in continent', one word doing two jobs: container indicator and the source of ASIA
annotationWithheld.clue: Food (or drink) initially making bloke randy or incontinent?

clue.text: 4 19 9's 22 17 in IOM with setter? No!

parts.note: IO looks like the Roman-style number ten and M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
the setter refers to himself as me
N is an abbreviation for no, as in number

explanation.surface: Asks whether the setter is on the Isle of Man, and answers no.
explanation.walkthrough: IOM looks like the Isle of Man, but read IO as 10 and M as 1000. The definition is the Duke's hill walkers from the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme the Grand Old Duke of York had that many soldiers, marched up a hill and down.

clue.text: Doing better as 17, as were 4 19 9's 11

definitions.meaning: beating others as walkers, covering ground faster on foot
the Duke's soldiers were marching out, up the hill and down again

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word in two: the men were out, marching.
explanation.definitionFit: Surpassing others on the march, and also describing troops going out on a march as in the rhyme.

clue.text: NB: Southeast Trains may be used for rail-flight connections

indicators.note: the letters may be used to make something else, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A notice says southeastern rail services can be used to connect with flights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be used' rearranges NB SE TRAINS. 'rail-flight' suggests trains and planes, but the rail is a handrail and the flight is a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Banisters are the uprights and handrail joining a staircase rail to the steps of the flight.

clue.text: Cover county before day's half over

parts.note: Beds is the short form of Bedfordshire, an English county
pre is a prefix meaning before

indicators.note: over says the letters are turned over and read the other way
half takes the first half of the word

explanation.surface: An instruction about covering the county before the day is half done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes DA from DAYS and 'over' turns it to AD. BEDS is Bedfordshire, a county north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative sheet laid over a bed is a cover for it.

clue.text: Sparkler turning heads in Italian town? Sparkler, anyway

indicators.note: turning says the collected letters are read in reverse order
the heads of words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A sparkling wine is named after an Italian town; it sparkles either way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads in' takes ITSA from the last four words and 'turning' reverses it. The clue is also a definition in its own right: the wine comes from an Italian town.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti spumante is a sparkling Italian wine, and a sparkler is crossword slang for fizzy wine.

clue.text: Reduction of a sort initially in order

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: a decree is an official order

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word sort

explanation.surface: A kind of cut is ordered by decree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives S from sort, and 'in' puts A plus S inside DECREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A decrease is a lessening in size or amount, which is a reduction.

clue.text: Winter sports event of which Spooner's dog sick?

indicators.note: Spooner's says the opening sounds of two words are exchanged, after the Reverend Spooner

parts.note: a hound is a hunting dog
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A skiing race in which the Reverend's dog falls ill.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, HOUND ILL runs as 'hown dill'; swapping the H and D sounds gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski race straight down a slope at speed is a standard alpine winter sports event.

clue.text: Those coming round include the prime of liveried footmen

indicators.note: include means the second piece is taken inside the first

parts.note: people coming round after sleep or a faint are wakers

indicators.note: the prime of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Liveried servants are among those being revived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the prime of' gives L from liveried and 'include' puts it inside WAKERS. 'footmen' suggests servants in livery but means people on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: People who travel on foot are walkers, so footmen in the literal sense.

clue.text: Racket due to fourth or fifth engagement?

parts.note: an engagement is a military battle
D is the fourth letter of the alphabet
taken as written
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A loud din results from the fourth or fifth battle of a war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' looks like noise, but it is a bat. The fourth and fifth letters of the alphabet are D and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A battledore is the small racket used in the old game of battledore and shuttlecock.

clue.text: See 4
English 16 22 runner with second language

parts.note: a ski is the runner used in a downhill race
a mo is a moment, a second

explanation.surface: An English downhill skier is paired with a second language.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 22 is the downhill answer elsewhere in the grid, and its runner is a ski.
explanation.definitionFit: Inuit and Yupik languages are collectively called by this name, so it denotes a language group.

clue.text: Carbohydrate found in cold chips a year after cooking

indicators.note: cooking changes what the ingredients look like, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Starch is detected in cold chips a year after they were fried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after cooking' rearranges COLD CHIPS A YEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch and cellulose are long chains of sugar units, carbohydrates of this kind.

clue.text: See 16
Reclusive boy taking issue to heart

indicators.note: taking means taking in, holding the other piece
to heart says it goes into the middle

parts.note: Eric is a boy's name
to emit is to issue, give out

explanation.surface: A boy takes a problem to heart and withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' and 'to heart' together say the issue goes into the middle of the boy's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Eremitic describes a hermit's way of life, living alone apart from society.

clue.text: Dog featuring in haiku? Lassie's back!

indicators.note: back says the hidden letters are read backwards
featuring in says the answer appears inside the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Lassie the film dog returns as the subject of a haiku.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Dog featuring' as the definition, but 'featuring in' is the hiding signal and 'Dog' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The saluki is a slender Middle Eastern sighthound breed.

clue.text: Forcibly remove dogs led astray, including setter

indicators.note: including means taking the other piece inside
led astray means wandering from the right path, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the setter refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Dogs wander off with the setter in tow and must be shifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges DOGS LED and 'including' puts I inside, after the D. 'setter' looks like a dog breed among the dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to force it out of its position.

clue.text: Happened to live by a 22

parts.note: to be is to exist, to live
a fell is a hill in northern England, 22 being HILL

explanation.surface: Something came about while living beside a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is HILL; a fell is the northern English word for a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Befell is the past tense of befall, meaning came to pass or occurred.
